subject: physics
question_text: Explain the effect of temperature on the viscosity of (a) liquids and (b) gases.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Mechanical Properties of Fluids, Very Short Answer Question 12, parts (a) and (b) (printed p.106). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. Part (a) asks about liquids and part (b) about gases; this card answers both parts as one 2-mark question, one mark per part. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: in a liquid, viscosity comes from the force holding neighbouring molecules together, and raising the temperature weakens that force, so the layers slide past each other more easily — viscosity falls. In a gas, viscosity comes from molecules crossing between layers and carrying momentum with them, and raising the temperature increases the molecular speed and so the rate of momentum transfer — viscosity rises.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Liquid: viscosity falls
steps.margin_note: First mark. Liquid: viscosity falls, and say why — weaker force between molecules.
steps.why: In a liquid, viscosity comes from the force holding neighbouring molecules together. A higher temperature weakens that force directly, so the layers move past each other more easily.
common_mistakes: Saying liquid viscosity rises with temperature. It falls — the opposite of a gas.
Giving the gas reason (faster molecules) for a liquid. In a liquid it is the weaker force between molecules, not molecular speed.

recall.must_convey: That a liquid's viscosity decreases as temperature rises, because the force between its molecules weakens and the layers slide past each other more easily.

steps.memory_tip: Liquid: hotter means weaker force between molecules, so viscosity falls.

steps.label: Gas: viscosity rises
lines: one layer to the next as they
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Gas: viscosity rises, and say why — faster molecules carry more momentum.
steps.why: In a gas, viscosity comes from molecules crossing between layers and carrying momentum with them. A higher temperature speeds up the molecules, so more momentum is carried across in the same time.
common_mistakes: Saying gas viscosity falls with temperature. It rises — the opposite of a liquid.
Giving the liquid reason (weaker intermolecular force) for a gas. In a gas it is faster molecules carrying momentum, not a weakening force.

recall.must_convey: That a gas's viscosity increases as temperature rises, because faster molecules carry more momentum between the layers.

steps.memory_tip: Gas: hotter means faster molecules, so they carry more momentum, so viscosity rises.

insider_note: One mark each, opposite directions: a liquid's viscosity falls with heat because the force between its molecules weakens; a gas's viscosity rises because its faster molecules carry more momentum between layers.
